newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish FinMin won't rule out wealth tax change.
newsitem.headline: Swedish FinMin won't rule out wealth tax change.

text.p: Sweden's Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said on Wednesday he did not rule out a change in wealth tax for main owners of companies listed on the Stockholm Stock Exchange's primary A list.

A 1996 law forces Swedes with wealth exceeding 900,000 crowns to pay 1.5 percent tax on 100 percent of the value of shares listed on the A list, up from 75 percent, while shares on the smaller O list remain exempt from tax.

The law has caused companies such as fashion retailer Hennes & Mauritz, media group Marieberg AB, construction group Lundbergs and investment company Latour to flee from the A to the O list this month.

The recent share transfers were triggered by a law adopted by parliament in June that says main shareholders -- people holding more than 25 percent of votes -- do not have to pay tax for shares listed on the A list after 1991.
Companies that started trading on the A list before 1991 had hoped parliament would change the 1996 law in connection with passing the new law but when this did not happen they moved.
Asbrink said the government did not intend to impose wealth tax on the bourse's smaller lists.
"We don't plan to introduce any wealth tax on the O and OTC (Over-The-Counter) lists," Asbrink told journalists in connection with a parliamentary debate.
But he did not rule out a change of the taxation of main owners on the A list.
"We follow the issue closely and it's possible that the situation requires some aftercare," Asbrink said.
No measures are currently on the agenda, he said, but added that it was not positive to have different tax pressures.
